1 ) The petitioner/State has challenged the order dated 12.05.2015 passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Rajnandgaon whereby the non-applicants have been discharged from the offence punishable under Section 306 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.

2) Facts of the present case are that on 14.02.2015, the mother of the deceased Smt. Ishwari Sahu lodged an FIR at Police Station Lalbag, District Rajnandgaon to the effect that her daughter, namely,
Madhuri Sahu was married to non-applicant No.1, namely Bhagwan Das Sahu and she was blessed with two children namely Sumesh aged about 7 years and Devsharan aged about 2 years.
It is further stated that her daughter had informed her father regarding the illicit relationship of her husband with non-applicant No.2.

On a fateful day i.e. 30.01.2015 the non-applicants forcibly entered the house of the deceased, which led to a quarrel between non-applicant No.1 and the deceased and the deceased was assaulted by non- applicant No.1 with hands and fists.
Thereafter, she committed suicide along with her son, namely, Sumesh by pouring kerosene and setting themselves ablaze.

sentences.text: On 30.01.2015, the deceased was admitted to the District Hospital, Rajnandgaon and thereafter, on 31.01.2015, her dying declaration was recorded by the Executive Magistrate, Raipur where she categorically stated that there was an illicit relationship between non-applicants No.1 and 2 and both entered into her house forcibly and that was the reason for suicide.

During the course of treatment, the deceased died on 03.02.2015 whereas, her son,
namely, Sumesh died on 30.02.2015.

The police prepared the spot map; recorded the statements of witnesses under Section 161 of Cr.P.C.; seized burned clothes, match-box, plastic containers etc.,
and on 15.02.2015, filed a charge sheet for the commission of offences punishable under Sections 498A and 306 read with Section 34 of IPC against the non-applicants.

The matter was heard by the learned trial Court on 12.05.2015 on framing of charge and the learned trial Court came to the conclusion that there are no ingredients of abetment and thus, discharged the non-applicants for the commission of offence punishable under Section 306 read with Section 34 of IPC.
With regard to Section 498A of IPC, the non-applicants were directed to appear before the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Rajnandgaon.

3) Learned counsel for the petitioner/State would submit that the learned trial Court was not justified in completely ignoring the oral evidence of family members of the deceased and without examining the ingredients of Section 107 of IPC the learned trial Court came to the conclusion that the ingredients of abetment are not available.

He would further submit that there is sufficient material to establish that there was an illicit relationship between non-applicants No.1 & 2 and just before the incident non- applicant No.1 came to his house along with non-applicant No.2 and there was an exchange of hot words and thereafter, the deceased was assaulted by non-applicant No.1 by hands and fists and thus the non-applicants instigated the deceased to commit suicide along with her son.
He would submit that the order passed by the learned trial Court is liable to be set aside.

4) On the other hand, learned counsel appearing for the non- applicants would submit that there was no abetment; there was no illicit relationship between non-applicants No.1 and 2; the deceased ought to have filed a complaint case for the commission of offences punishable under Sections 494 & 495 of IPC but she took a drastic decision to commit suicide, which cannot be termed as a result of abetment.

They would submit that the learned trial Court has rightly discharged the non- applicants for the commission of an offence punishable under Section 306 read with Section 34 of IPC and directed them to appear before the Chief Judicial Magistrate for trial.
5) I have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the record with utmost circumspection.
6) From the perusal of the record, it appears that the deceased was married to non-applicant No.1 and they were blessed with two issues.
It was alleged that there was extramarital affair of non- applicant No.1 with non-applicant No.2 and this fact was disclosed by someone to the deceased.
7) A village meeting was convened and non-applicant No.1 was advised to leave non-applicant No.2 and stay peacefully along with the deceased.

On 30.01.2015, non-applicant No.1 came to his house along with non-applicant No.2 and there was some quarrel between the deceased and non-applicant No.1, thereafter, the deceased was assaulted by non-applicant No.1.

The deceased committed suicide along with his elder son by pouring kerosene and setting themselves ablaze and both were admitted The State Of Chhattisgarh vs Bhagwan Das Sahu on 17 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/113736921/

sentences.text: As per the medical report, there were 86% deep burn injuries over the body of the deceased.
During the course of treatment, her dying declaration was recorded by the Executive Magistrate, Raipur on 31.01.2015 at about 6:20 pm after getting the Medical Officer's approval.
The dying declaration was signed by the deceased, where she has made serious allegations against the non-applicants.
Deceased/ Madhuri Sahu died on 03.02.2015 and later on, her son also died on 30.02.2015.
During the course of the investigation, the police prepared a site plan.
Postmortem of the dead body was conducted by the doctor and the cause of death was cardio- respiratory failure as a result of burn injuries and their complications.

The statements of the witnesses were recorded where Smt. Ishwari Sahu - mother of the deceased, Lakhan Sahu - father of the deceased, Ku. Anita Sahu - sister of the deceased, Smt. Jamuna Bai - neighbour of the deceased, Kritram Sahu, Kranti Kumar Sahu, Dilip Sahu, Yogendra Sahu, Romnath and Arjun Sahu - villagers have categorically stated that the deceased committed suicide on account of abetment.
8) Sections 107 & 306 of IPC are reproduced hereinbelow for ready reference:

"107. Abetment of a thing.--A person abets the doing of a thing, who-- (First) -- Instigates any person to do that thing; or (Secondly) --Engages with one or more other person or persons in any conspiracy for the doing of that thing, if an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that conspiracy, and in order to the doing of that thing; or (Thirdly) -- Intentionally aids, by any act or illegal omission,
the doing of that thing.
306. Abetment of suicide.--If any person commits suicide, whoever abets the commission of such suicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine."
9) The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the matter of M. Arjunan v. State, represented by its Inspector of Police, reported in (2019) 3 SCC 315, has summarized the ingredients of Section 306 of IPC.
The relevant paragraph is reproduced herein below:
"(7) The essential ingredients of the offence under Section 306 I.P.C. are: (i) the abetment; (ii) the intention of the accused to aid or instigate or abet the deceased to commit suicide.
The act of the accused, however, insulting the deceased by using abusive language will not, by itself, constitute the abetment of suicide.
There should be evidence capable of suggesting that the accused intended by such act to instigate the deceased to commit suicide.

Unless the ingredients of instigation/abetment to commit suicide are satisfied, accused cannot be convicted under Section 306 I.P.C."
10)

In the matter of Ude Singh & Ors. vs. State of Haryana, reported in (2019) 17 SCC 301, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that in case of alleged abetment of suicide, there must be proof of direct or indirect act/s of incitement to the commission of suicide.

sentences.text: In cases of alleged abetment of suicide, there must be a proof of direct or indirect act/s of incitement to the commission of suicide.

It could hardly be disputed that the question of cause of a suicide, particularly in the context of an offence of abetment of suicide, remains a vexed one, involving multifaceted and complex attributes of human behaviour and responses/reactions.
In the case of accusation for abetment of suicide, the Court would be looking for cogent and convincing proof of the act/s of incitement to the commission of suicide.

In the case of suicide, mere allegation of harassment of the deceased by another person would not suffice unless there be such action on the part of the accused which compels the person to commit suicide; and such an offending action ought to be proximate to the time of occurrence.
Whether a person has abetted in the commission of suicide by another or not, could only be gathered from the facts and circumstances of each case.
16.1 For the purpose of finding out if a person has abetted commission of suicide by another, the consideration would be if the accused is guilty of the act of instigation of the act of suicide.
As explained and reiterated by this Court in the decisions above-referred, instigation means to goad, urge forward, provoke, incite or encourage to do an act.

If the persons who committed suicide had been hypersensitive and the action of accused is otherwise not ordinarily expected to induce a similarly circumstanced person to commit suicide, it may not be safe to hold the accused guilty of abetment of suicide.

But, on the other hand, if the accused by his acts and by his continuous course of conduct creates a situation which leads the deceased perceiving no other option except to commit suicide, the case may fall within the four-corners of Section 306 IPC.

If the accused plays an active role in tarnishing the self-esteem and self-respect of the victim, which eventually draws the victim to commit suicide, the accused may be held guilty of abetment of suicide.

The question of mens rea on the part of the accused in such cases would be examined with reference to the actual acts and deeds of the accused and if the acts and deeds are only of such nature where the accused intended nothing more than harassment or snap show of anger, a particular case may fall short of the offence of abetment of suicide.
However, if the accused kept on irritating or annoying the deceased by words or deeds until the deceased reacted or was provoked, a particular case may be that of abetment of suicide.

Such being the matter of delicate analysis of human behaviour, each case is required to be examined on its own facts, while taking note of all the surrounding factors having bearing on the actions and psyche of the accused and the deceased."
11)

In the matter of S.S. Chheena v. Vijay Kumar Mahajan and Another, reported in (2010) 12 SCC 190, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in paragraph 25 held as under:
"25. Abetment involves a mental process of instigating a person or intentionally aiding a person in doing of a thing. Without a positive act on the part of the accused to instigate or aid in committing suicide, conviction cannot be sustained.

sentences.text: The court must ensure that criminal prosecution is not used as an instrument of harassment or for seeking private vendetta or with an ulterior motive to pressurize the accused.
On analysis of the aforementioned cases, we are of the opinion that it is neither possible nor desirable to lay down an inflexible rule that would govern the exercise of inherent jurisdiction.

Inherent jurisdiction of the High Courts under Section 482 CrPC though wide has to be exercised sparingly, carefully and with caution and only when it is justified by the tests specifically laid down in the statute itself and in the aforementioned cases.
In view of the settled legal position, the impugned judgment cannot be sustained."
35. It is a well settled proposition of law that criminal prosecution, if otherwise justified, is not vitiated on account of malafides or vendetta.
As said by Krishna Iyer, J. in State of Punjab v. Gurdial Singh "if the use of the power for the fulfillment of a legitimate object the actuation or catalysation by malice is not legicidal."

sentences.text: 13) In light of the judgments passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, it is quite clear that the deceased was the married wife of non- applicant No.1; he developed an extramarital affair with non- applicant No.2 during subsistence of his first marriage.
He came along with non-applicant No.2 in his house where the deceased was staying along with her children.
There was a quarrel and the deceased was assaulted in the presence of her children and thereafter, she took the decision to commit suicide along with her elder son.

It was not the first instance and even earlier there was a complaint with regard to extramarital affair of non-applicant No.1 and a meeting was held in the village where he was advised to leave that lady/non-applicant No.2.

Instead of leaving, he provoked the deceased and entered the house along with non- applicant No.2 and thus, non-applicant No.1 by his acts and conduct created a situation that led the deceased perceiving no other option except to commit suicide and therefore, the case would fall within the four corners of Section 306 of IPC.
It further appears that the non-applicants had played an active role in instigating the deceased for committing suicide.

Instigation means to goad, urge forward, provoke, incite or encourage to do an act where such an action on the part of the accused compels the person to commit suicide; and such an offending action ought to be proximate to the time of occurrence, in such circumstances it can safely be held that the suicide committed by that person is a result of alleged abetment.
Accordingly, in the opinion of this Court, the learned trial Court has committed an error of law in discharging non-applicants No.1 and 2.
